comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C4, C28-C32, C36-C38 regarding Sepw1-Cre line characterization and ablation validation. Both evaluations find the histological validation and specificity well-supported with no concerns raised.

Strong agreement on claims C5, C7-C8, C33, C35, C43-C48, C56, C66 regarding ablation behavioral effects. Both find increased dark zone speed and reduced rest time well-supported. OpenEval includes additional claims (C39-C42) about preserved dark preference that peer review addresses separately in R3.

Substantial overlap on transition speed and BIL effects (C49, C51-C55). OpenEval focuses on statistical modeling of transition speeds, while peer review also includes basic behavioral characterization (C6, C39-C42) that OpenEval addresses in R2. Both find evidence supported.

Perfect agreement on claims C57-C64 regarding LL/DD control experiments. Both evaluations find these controls essential for establishing valence-dependent effects and accept the lack of group differences in homogeneous conditions.

Strong agreement on calcium imaging findings (C67-C78). Both find zone preference and speed tuning well-characterized. OpenEval raises interpretive concerns about negative speed relationships, while peer review also includes claims C9-C10 and C79-C82 (ROC analysis) that OpenEval addresses separately in R6.

Partial overlap on ROC analysis (C79-C82). OpenEval finds deceleration prediction well-supported. Peer review groups this with broader imaging results (R5), while OpenEval separates ROC analysis from basic activity characterization.

Strong agreement on transition-specific neural activity (C83-C91). Both find statistical associations between transition activity and zone/speed relationships well-supported. OpenEval separates this from temporal dynamics (R8), while peer review groups all transition analyses together.

Partial overlap on temporal dynamics of calcium activity (C92-C95). OpenEval raises concerns about miniscope effects on behavior, while peer review groups temporal analysis with broader transition findings. Both ultimately support the data quality.

Strong agreement on projection-specific photometry (C96-C103). Both find SNr specificity well-demonstrated through systematic comparison across target nuclei. OpenEval separates anatomical/basic photometry from detailed cross-correlation analysis (R10).

Strong agreement on cross-correlation analysis (C104-C111). Both find temporal relationships and negative acceleration lag convincing. Peer review groups this with basic projection findings (R7), while OpenEval separates detailed temporal analysis.

Perfect agreement on patchy vs. matrix comparison (C112-C118). Both find the functional distinction well-supported by differential speed/acceleration correlations. Both note the importance of this comparison for establishing specificity.

Substantial agreement on chemogenetic experiments (C119-C125). Both find Gq suppression and preserved valence discrimination supported. Peer review also includes claims C11, C13 about general chemogenetic approach and broader behavioral effects (C126-C135) that OpenEval addresses separately in R13-R14.

Strong agreement on Gq effects on speed distributions and transitions (C126-C131). Both find effects opposite to ablation, supporting causality. OpenEval notes speculative interpretation of 'anxiety-related vigor,' while peer review accepts the causal demonstration.

Agreement on LL/DD chemogenetic controls (C132-C135). Both find valence-dependent effects consistent across ablation and activation. Peer review groups all chemogenetic results together, while OpenEval separates control experiments.

Strong agreement on optogenetic SNr terminal manipulation (C136-C147). Both find preserved valence discrimination with altered transition speeds. OpenEval notes weaker effects than DREADDs and questions sufficiency interpretation, while peer review accepts the findings without concern.

Perfect agreement on patchy vs. matrix optogenetic comparison (C148-C159). Both find differential effects strongly support functional specificity and balance model. Both note that matrix activation mimics patchy ablation.

Strong agreement on major conclusions (C160, C163-C164, C168, C170, C172). Both affirm novelty, significance, and challenge to traditional views. Peer review also includes claims C15, C34, C171 about broader impact that OpenEval addresses contextually.

Agreement on mechanistic speculation (C173-C179). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct testing, while peer review accepts discussion as appropriate speculation. Both acknowledge these mechanisms are literature-based rather than empirically tested in this study.

Agreement on interpretation of activity pattern differences (C180-C186). OpenEval finds balance model supported but notes considerable inference, while peer review accepts the interpretation. Both acknowledge complexity and heterogeneity within patchy neurons.

Agreement on miniscope limitations (C187-C189). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to loss of BIL effect and untested stress hypothesis. Peer review acknowledges this limitation while accepting overall imaging results as valuable.

Agreement on reconciling zone preference and event frequency findings (C190-C194). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN with plausible but speculative resolution. Peer review accepts the complexity and heterogeneity discussion without specific concern.

Perfect agreement on technical limitations and alternative interpretations (C195-C204). Both find the discussion thorough and honest. Peer review explicitly notes that limitations are appropriately discussed and accepts the transparent approach.

Agreement on broader functional interpretations (C205-C213). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature of anxiety, attention, and habit connections. Peer review accepts discussion as appropriate for broader implications without raising concerns.

Agreement on translational implications and future directions (C214-C215). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN but reasonable speculation. Peer review notes broad interest across neuroscience fields, consistent with accepting the discussion of potential significance.
